chapter: In The Mood, Rendezvous and Capitol
title: Joe Garland's saxophone exercise and Louis Armstrong's refusal
summary: Love explains that Garland wrote In The Mood as an exercise; Armstrong would not touch it, and Plas Johnson's tenor on the rock version is praised.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Yeah. But the public appearance was me and that's how I made so much and then the next thing about it, Joe Garland, he helped push it and them when I was on Cash Box--I mean Bandstand, he helped get them in. You see, I just went up there myself and Joe Garland helped get the men together.
Did you know that Joe wrote that as a saxophone exercise?
He told me also he tried to get Louie, and Louie said, oh, it's not any vocal, I want something I can kind of jive and he wouldn't fool with it.

They considered it as kind of a corny number, which it was, because it was just a saxophone exercise, but they couldn't anticipate how big it would be, and so naturally--I heard Count Basie play it in 1938, the same year that it was so very popular, thirty eight or thirty nine, Earl Warren in the reed section just tripped on out and they made it likeable; but the rock version you made, that Plas was marvelous.
Yeah, that's what I had this little deal that I said, when I was reading that to you, I consider him responsible for that hit. I have it on something about that.
